It's been a week, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup, much has happened. I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course. I've been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. There was much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how {~~participate~>to participate~~} in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won't try to find a clever Agile analogy from this.

If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI-related topics this week, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).

## Canadian Government AI Strategy
Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and invest in Canadian AI companies.

The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity". When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I'm sure we've all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.

The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).

Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.

I'm also thinking that we will see a lot of "AI Washing" in the next few years. Changes that were already in progress will be rebranded as AI. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.

## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: Just use agents and don’t worry next week's model will solve all the existing problems.

I've had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.

### Fable Security Audit
Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s experience with Fable, its strength is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect: it used up my whole Claude subscription for a 5hr period and required another block later that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 

The frontier labs don't generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi 3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8[^kimi-opus]. The Kimi 3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters[^kimi-params]. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.

### Opus Research Task
I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my 5hr block and needed another block later that evening to finish the task.

For that much compute, I was expecting a nice long report with real depth. Instead, I got a 3-page report with two good insights.

Agents are not necessarily better. I may well need a much longer blog post to explain why. The short version: assume each agent is imperfect at the task. You can't mask the imperfections of one agent with another. If anything, I would expect the imperfections to multiply.

## Big Ask
One of the two insights from Opus's Research Task? Ask your newsletter readers for referrals. To quote Opus: "single most effective newsletter growth strategy is **direct recommendations from existing subscribers (word-of-mouth/referral)**". I'm supposed to offer you a discount or a free trial in return. In practice, I can't see what I would offer at the moment.

===== 2026-07-08-too-much-work-in-progress-too-little-getting-done.md =====
## Reading Rabbit Hole
- [LLMs Corrupt Your Documents When You Delegate](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.15597v1) - Philippe Laban, Tobias Schnabel, Jennifer Neville and [Further Notes on Our Recent Research on AI Delegation and Long-Horizon Reliability](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/further-notes-on-our-recent-research-on-ai-delegation-and-long-horizon-reliability/) the authors explore what happens when you delegate the work on a document to an LLM over a series of iterations. *It's not pretty, unless you're willing to accept results that are more than a little off.*
- [Understanding LLMs’ Reasoning Limits Today: Insights to Shape Your Strategy](https://medium.com/@parserdigital/understanding-llms-reasoning-limits-today-insights-to-shape-your-future-strategy-fc1c27c9e904) - Ricardo Moral - examines the different types of human reasoning strategies and how LLMs perform on them. Key takeaway: they mimic many types of human reasoning, without any understanding. Result: they make logical mistakes; can’t extrapolate beyond their training data etc.
- [Unhealthy code is burning your token usage](https://codescene.com/blog/unhealthy-code-is-burning-your-token-usage-heres-the-data) - Adam Tornhill - Unhealthy code requires models to do more work in response to a prompt. As LLM tokens are about to get more expensive, code health will really matter.

Cheers,
Mark

1

3	It's been a week, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup, much has happened. I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course. I've been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. There was much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how to participate in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won't try to find a clever Agile analogy from this.
4	
5	If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI-related topics this week, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).
6	
7	## Canadian Government AI Strategy
8	Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and investing in Canadian AI companies.
9	
10	The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity". When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I'm sure we've all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.
11	
12	The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).
13	
14	Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.
15	
16	I'm also thinking that we will see a lot of "AI Washing" in the next few years. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.
17	
18	## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
19	In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: next week's model (Fable) will solve all the existing problems and use agents to offset other agents mistakes (Opus).
20	
21	I've had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.
22	
23	### Fable Security Audit
24	Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s experience with Fable, its strength is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect: it used up my entire daily usage limit, and I had to wait for it to reset that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 
25	
26	The frontier labs don't generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi K3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8[^kimi-opus]. The Kimi K3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters[^kimi-params]. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.
27	
28	### Opus Research Task
29	I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my usage limit and needed another block later that evening to finish the task.
30	
31	For that much compute, I was expecting a nice long report with real depth. Instead, I got a 3-page report with two good insights.
32	
33	Agents are not necessarily better. I may well need a much longer blog post to explain why. The short version: assume each agent is imperfect at the task. You can't mask the imperfections of one agent with another. If anything, I would expect the imperfections to multiply.
34

To quote Opus: "single most effective newsletter growth strategy is **direct recommendations from existing subscribers (word-of-mouth/referral)**". I'm supposed to offer you a discount or a free trial in return. In practice, I can't see what I would offer at the moment.

It's been a week, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup, much has happened. I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course. I've been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. There was much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how to participate in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won't try to find a clever Agile analogy from this.

If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI-related topics this week, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).

## Canadian Government AI Strategy
Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and investing in Canadian AI companies.

The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity". When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I'm sure we've all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.

The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).

Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.

I'm also thinking that we will see a lot of "AI Washing" in the next few years. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.

## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: next week's model (Fable) will solve all the existing problems and use agents to offset other agents mistakes (Opus).

I've had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.

### Fable Security Audit
Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s experience with Fable, its strength is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect: it used up my entire daily usage limit, and I had to wait for it to reset that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 

The frontier labs don't generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi K3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8[^kimi-opus]. The Kimi K3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters[^kimi-params]. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.

### Opus Research Task
I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It's been a week, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup, much has happened. I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course. I've been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. There was much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how to participate in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won't try to find a clever Agile analogy from this.

If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI-related topics this week, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).

## Canadian Government AI Strategy
Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and investing in Canadian AI companies.

The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity". When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I'm sure we've all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.

The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).

Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.

I'm also thinking that we will see a lot of "AI Washing" in the next few years. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.

## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: next week's model (Fable) will solve all the existing problems and use agents to offset other agents mistakes (Opus).

I've had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.

### Fable Security Audit
Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s experience with Fable, its strength is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect: it used up my entire daily usage limit, and I had to wait for it to reset that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 

The frontier labs don't generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi K3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8[^kimi-opus]. The Kimi K3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters[^kimi-params]. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.

### Opus Research Task
I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my usage limit and needed another block later that evening to finish the task.

For that much compute, I was expecting a nice long report with real depth. Instead, I got a 3-page report with two good insights.

Agents are not necessarily better. I may well need a much longer blog post to explain why. The short version: assume each agent is imperfect at the task. You can't mask the imperfections of one agent with another. If anything, I would expect the imperfections to multiply.

To quote Opus: "single most effective newsletter growth strategy is **direct recommendations from existing subscribers (word-of-mouth/referral)**". {~~It's been a week, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup, much has happened.~>The past couple of weeks have been full, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup.~~} I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course. I've been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. There was much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how to participate in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won't try to find a clever Agile analogy from this.{++ GenAI gives me plenty to noodle on, so let's go there instead.++}

If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI-related topics {~~this week~>in this issue~~}, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).

## Canadian Government AI Strategy
Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and investing in Canadian AI companies.

The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity". When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I'm sure we've all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.

The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).

Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.

I'm also thinking that we will see a lot of "AI Washing" in the next few years. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.

## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: next week's model (Fable) will solve all the existing problems and use agents to offset other agents mistakes (Opus).

I've had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.

### Fable Security Audit
Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s experience with Fable, its strength is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect: it used up my entire daily usage limit, and I had to wait for it to reset that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 

The frontier labs don't generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi K3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8[^kimi-opus]. The Kimi K3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters[^kimi-params]. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.

### Opus Research Task
I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my usage limit and needed another block later that evening to finish the task.

For that much compute, I was expecting a nice long report with real depth. Instead, I got a 3-page report with two good insights.

Agents are not necessarily better. I may well need a much longer blog post to explain why. The short version: assume each agent is imperfect at the task. You can't mask the imperfections of one agent with another. If anything, I would expect the imperfections to multiply.

## Big Ask
One of the two insights from Opus's Research Task? Ask your newsletter readers for referrals. To quote Opus: "single most effective newsletter growth strategy is **direct recommendations from existing subscribers (word-of-mouth/referral)**". I'm supposed to offer you a discount or a free trial in return. In practice, I can't see what I would offer at the moment.

If you get value from this newsletter, please share it with a friend. If someone shared it with you, click here to subscribe.{>>Claude: This referral ask doubles as your reader CTA and ties to the issue's theme - good. Just make sure "click here" gets a real subscribe link before send.<<}

lines: The frontier labs don't generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi K3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8[^kimi-opus]. The Kimi K3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters[^kimi-params]. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.
### Opus Research Task

-I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my usage limit and needed another block later that evening to finish the task.
